query.explanation: The WHATWG URL parser treats a backslash exactly like a forward slash for special schemes such as https. So "/\\evil.com/admin" is parsed as "//evil.com/admin", a protocol-relative URL, and the parser starts a brand new authority instead of keeping the base host. The resolved hostname is evil.com, not example.com. This is why a redirect check that only verifies the target "starts with /" is unsafe: both "//evil.com" and "/\\evil.com" pass that test yet send the browser off site. Validate by resolving the target against your own origin and comparing url.origin (or url.hostname) to an allowlist.
query.title: Backslashes in redirect targets

questions.prompt: Which directive applies to image loads under the policy below?

choices.rationale: script-src only restricts script resources; it is never consulted for image loads.
The policy contains no img-src directive, so there is nothing to apply.
Missing fetch directives inherit default-src, so images are still restricted.

query.explanation: Fetch directives that are absent from a policy fall back to default-src. Since img-src is not listed, image loads are checked against default-src 'self'. script-src is explicitly present, so it overrides default-src for scripts only, and it never applies to images.
query.title: default-src fallback

questions.prompt: Is an inline <script> with no nonce attribute blocked by the policy below?

query.explanation: When a script-src source list contains a nonce or a hash, user agents ignore 'unsafe-inline'. That makes the policy nonce-only, so an inline script without the matching nonce is blocked. The keyword is kept in real policies purely as a fallback for very old browsers.
query.title: Nonces disable 'unsafe-inline'

questions.rationale: 'unsafe-inline' is ignored whenever a nonce or hash source is present, so the inline script is not allowed to run.

questions.prompt: Which header name delivers a content security policy in report-only mode?

choices.rationale: This header enforces the policy and blocks violations rather than only reporting them.
An obsolete vendor-prefixed name; it is not the report-only header in any current browser.
No such header exists; reporting mode uses the -Report-Only suffix.

query.explanation: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only carries a policy that is monitored and reported but never enforced, which makes it the safe way to trial a policy. Content-Security-Policy is the enforcing header, and the X- prefixed name is a long-obsolete vendor spelling.
query.title: Report-only header

questions.prompt: Does frame-ancestors fall back to default-src when the policy omits it?

query.explanation: Only fetch directives such as script-src, img-src and connect-src fall back to default-src. frame-ancestors is a navigation/document directive, so omitting it leaves embedding unrestricted no matter how strict default-src is.
query.title: Which directives inherit default-src

questions.rationale: frame-ancestors is not a fetch directive, so it never inherits default-src and must be stated explicitly to restrict framing.

questions.prompt: Which request URL does the policy below allow?

choices.rationale: The source pins the https scheme, so a plain http request to the same host is blocked.
The host must match exactly; example.com is not cdn.example.com.
Without a leading *., extra subdomain labels do not match the host-source.

query.explanation: A host-source with an explicit scheme matches only that scheme and exactly that host; the path is unconstrained when the source lists none. So http:// is rejected, a different host is rejected, and extra subdomain labels are rejected because the source has no leading wildcard.
query.title: Host-source matching

questions.prompt: On the page below, does script-src 'self' allow https://cdn.example.com/a.js?

query.explanation: 'self' matches the document's own origin: the same scheme, host and port. A subdomain such as cdn.example.com is a different origin, so its script is blocked. Allowing it requires listing the host explicitly or using a wildcard host-source.
query.title: What 'self' means

questions.rationale: 'self' is an exact origin match, and cdn.example.com is a different host from example.com, so the script is blocked.

questions.prompt: Which script URL does the policy below allow?

choices.rationale: *.example.com requires at least one extra label; the bare host example.com does not match it.
The real host here is evil.net, which does not end with .example.com.
The wildcard needs a dot boundary, so notexample.com is not a subdomain match.

query.explanation: A *. prefix matches hosts that end with the remaining labels preceded by a dot, so cdn.example.com matches. The bare registrable domain example.com does not match its own wildcard, and lookalike hosts such as example.com.evil.net or notexample.com fail the dotted-suffix test.
query.title: Wildcard host-sources

questions.prompt: Which sources does script-src list in the policy below?

choices.rationale: 'none' is the source list of default-src, which is overridden for scripts by the explicit script-src.
The source list has two entries; the CDN host is part of script-src too.
That is the whole policy string, not the source list belonging to script-src.

query.explanation: A policy can be delivered in a meta http-equiv element, and each directive is a space-separated name plus source list, separated from the next by a semicolon. Parsing the content attribute yields script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; default-src 'none' applies only to directives that are absent.
query.title: Policies delivered by meta

questions.prompt: Does the policy below block a call to eval() made by page JavaScript?

query.explanation: String-to-code APIs such as eval and new Function are permitted only when script-src includes 'unsafe-eval'. 'unsafe-inline' is a separate keyword that governs inline <script> blocks and inline event handlers, so it does not re-enable eval.
query.title: 'unsafe-eval'

questions.rationale: Without 'unsafe-eval' in script-src, eval is refused; 'unsafe-inline' only covers inline scripts and handlers.

questions.prompt: Which directive states which sites may embed this page in a frame?

choices.rationale: frame-src limits the URLs this page can load into its own frames, not who may frame it.
child-src is a fallback for frames and workers the page creates; it says nothing about its embedders.
default-src only backs up fetch directives and never applies to frame-ancestors.

query.explanation: frame-ancestors is checked by the browser when another document tries to embed this one, making it the CSP replacement for X-Frame-Options. frame-src and child-src instead restrict the URLs this page may load into frames or workers it creates.
query.title: Restricting embedding

questions.prompt: Does the Secure attribute hide a cookie from document.cookie?

query.explanation: Secure only restricts the cookie to HTTPS connections; it says nothing about script access. HttpOnly is the attribute that removes a cookie from document.cookie, so a Secure-but-not-HttpOnly session cookie is still stealable by XSS.
query.title: Secure vs HttpOnly

questions.rationale: A Secure cookie is still exposed to page scripts through document.cookie; only HttpOnly keeps it out of JavaScript's reach.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute keeps a cookie out of document.cookie?

choices.rationale: Secure limits the cookie to HTTPS requests but leaves it readable by document.cookie.
SameSite controls whether the cookie rides on cross-site requests, not whether scripts can read it.
Path narrows which URL paths the cookie is sent to; it does not hide the cookie from JavaScript.

query.explanation: HttpOnly tells the browser to expose the cookie only on HTTP requests, never to the document.cookie API. Secure, SameSite and Path control transport, cross-site sending and URL scope respectively, not script visibility.
query.title: Attribute that blocks script access

questions.prompt: What does document.cookie return after the browser stores the cookie below?

choices.rationale: Attributes are never echoed back by document.cookie; only the name=value pair is readable.
Path is stored by the browser but is not part of the document.cookie string.
document.cookie returns the full name=value pair, not just the cookie name.

query.explanation: The cookie store keeps attributes like Path, Max-Age, Secure and SameSite internally. Reading document.cookie yields only the name=value pairs, separated by '; ', so scripts can never inspect a cookie's attributes.
query.title: document.cookie exposes only name=value

questions.prompt: Which SameSite value allows a cookie on cross-site subresource requests?

choices.rationale: Strict withholds the cookie from every cross-site request, including subresources.
Lax sends the cookie only on top-level cross-site navigations, not on cross-site subresource requests.
Secure is a separate attribute, not a legal SameSite value, so this would be ignored.

query.explanation: SameSite=None opts the cookie out of same-site restrictions entirely, so it is attached to cross-site requests. Lax allows it only on top-level cross-site navigations, and Strict blocks all cross-site sending. 'Secure' is not a SameSite value.
query.title: SameSite values

questions.prompt: Must a cookie with SameSite=None also set Secure to be accepted?

query.explanation: Modern browsers reject a Set-Cookie header that declares SameSite=None without the Secure attribute, because a cookie travelling on cross-site requests must at least be confined to HTTPS.
query.title: SameSite=None requires Secure

questions.rationale: Without Secure the browser drops a SameSite=None cookie entirely, so the pair of attributes must always be set together.

questions.prompt: Can a page on sub.example.com set a cookie with Domain=example.com?

query.explanation: A host may set a cookie for itself or for any parent domain that is not a public suffix, and the cookie then applies to that domain and all of its subdomains. It may not set cookies for unrelated domains or for a registry suffix like 'com'.
query.title: Domain attribute scope

questions.rationale: example.com is a parent of sub.example.com and is not a public suffix, so the browser accepts the cookie and shares it across all example.com subdomains.

questions.prompt: Which request path receives a cookie stored with Path=/app?

choices.rationale: A prefix match is not enough: the character after the cookie path must be '/', and here it is 'l'.
The root path is shorter than /app, so it does not begin with the cookie path.
Path matching compares from the start of the path, and this path does not begin with /app.

query.explanation: Path matching requires the request path to equal the cookie path, or to begin with it followed by a '/'. So /app/settings matches Path=/app, while /apple only shares a character prefix and is not a path match.
query.title: Cookie path matching

questions.prompt: Does a Set-Cookie header with Max-Age=0 delete the cookie right away?

query.explanation: Max-Age=0 (or any negative value, or a past Expires date) marks the cookie as already expired, so the browser removes it from the store immediately. This is the standard way a server clears a session cookie on logout.
query.title: Deleting cookies with Max-Age=0

questions.rationale: A non-positive Max-Age makes the cookie expire at once rather than storing it for zero extra time, so the browser drops it instead of keeping it as a session cookie.

questions.prompt: Which Set-Cookie value creates a cookie discarded when the browser closes?

choices.rationale: Max-Age gives the cookie a one-hour lifetime, so it is persistent and survives a browser restart.
An Expires date in the future makes the cookie persistent until that date.
Max-Age=0 tells the browser to delete the cookie right away rather than keep it for the session.

query.explanation: A cookie becomes persistent only when the server supplies a lifetime, either with `Max-Age` (seconds) or `Expires` (a date). If neither attribute is present, the cookie is a session cookie: the browser keeps it in memory and drops it when the browsing session ends. `Max-Age=0` (or a past Expires date) is the opposite extreme — it tells the browser to delete the cookie immediately. Session cookies are often preferred for short-lived authentication because nothing is left on disk.
query.title: Session cookies vs persistent cookies

questions.prompt: Which response header names the origin allowed to read a cross-origin response?

choices.rationale: Origin is sent by the browser on the request; it does not grant read access to the response.
That header lists request headers accepted during a preflight, not which origin may read the body.
That header only says how long a preflight result may be cached.

query.explanation: The browser only hands a cross-origin response to JavaScript if the response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin with either `*` or the exact requesting origin. Access-Control-Allow-Headers and Access-Control-Max-Age are preflight-only answers, and Origin is a request header the browser sends.
query.title: The CORS allow-origin header

questions.prompt: Does Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * permit a credentialed cross-origin fetch?

query.explanation: With credentials (cookies or HTTP auth) the wildcard is rejected: the response must echo the exact origin and also send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The answer is False because `*` is treated as invalid for credentialed requests, so the browser blocks the response.
query.title: Wildcard origin and credentials

questions.rationale: A credentialed request requires the exact origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; the wildcard is rejected, so True is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method does a CORS preflight request use?

choices.rationale: HEAD is a normal request method; it is never used to ask permission for another request.
POST would send a body and perform the action, which is exactly what a preflight must avoid.
TRACE is a diagnostic method unrelated to CORS and is usually disabled.

query.explanation: The preflight is always an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and, when needed, Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server answers it without running the real operation.
query.title: The preflight method

questions.prompt: Which response header lets page JS read the X-Total-Count response header?

choices.rationale: That header allows headers on the outgoing request, not reading of response headers.
It permits reading the body, but custom response headers stay hidden without an expose list.
It only controls preflight caching and has no effect on header visibility.

query.explanation: Cross-origin JavaScript can only read a small safelist of response headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, and a few others). Any other header, such as X-Total-Count, must be named in Access-Control-Expose-Headers before response.headers.get() returns it.
query.title: Exposing response headers

questions.prompt: Which preflight request header names the real request's HTTP method?

choices.rationale: That is the server's reply listing permitted methods, not the browser's question.
That header lists header names the real request will send, not its method.
This is an application-level tunnelling convention, not part of the CORS protocol.

query.explanation: The OPTIONS preflight describes the pending request with Access-Control-Request-Method (the method) and Access-Control-Request-Headers (the non-safelisted header names). The server replies with the matching Access-Control-Allow-* headers.
query.title: Preflight request headers

questions.prompt: Does a cross-origin GET with no custom headers trigger a preflight request?

query.explanation: A GET with only safelisted headers is a simple request: the browser sends it straight away and then decides, from Access-Control-Allow-Origin, whether JavaScript may read the response. The answer is False because no OPTIONS round trip is involved.
query.title: Simple requests skip the preflight

questions.rationale: Preflights are only sent for non-simple methods or non-safelisted headers, so claiming True would misdescribe a plain GET.

questions.prompt: Which URL is cross-origin relative to a page at https://app.example.com/a?

choices.rationale: Only the path differs, and paths are not part of an origin.
443 is the default https port, so this is the same origin written explicitly.
Query strings are not part of an origin.

query.explanation: An origin is scheme + host + port. Paths and query strings are irrelevant, and https://app.example.com:443 is the same origin because 443 is the default port for https. Switching the scheme to http changes the origin, so such a request needs CORS.
query.title: Origin comparison

questions.prompt: Does Access-Control-Max-Age let the browser skip repeat preflights for a while?

query.explanation: Access-Control-Max-Age gives the lifetime in seconds of the preflight result cache entry for that origin, URL, method and header set. While the entry is fresh the browser reuses it instead of sending another OPTIONS request, so the answer is True.
query.title: Caching preflight results

questions.rationale: False would imply every request repeats the OPTIONS round trip, but a fresh cache entry suppresses it until the max-age expires.

questions.prompt: Which POST Content-Type value avoids a CORS preflight?

choices.rationale: JSON is not on the safelist, so a POST with it is preflighted.
XML is not a safelisted Content-Type, so the browser preflights the request.
Only text/plain is safelisted among text types; text/html triggers a preflight.

query.explanation: Only three Content-Type values keep a POST simple: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data and text/plain. Anything else, including application/json, forces an OPTIONS preflight.
query.title: Safelisted Content-Type values

questions.prompt: Which request header names the origin of the page making a cross-origin fetch?

choices.rationale: Referer may carry the full page URL including path and query, and it can be suppressed or trimmed by referrer policy, so it is not the CORS origin header.
Host names the server being contacted (the request's own target), not the origin of the page issuing the request.
That is a response header sent by the server to state which origin may read the response; browsers never send it on a request.

query.explanation: On cross-origin requests (and on preflights), the browser automatically attaches `Origin`, whose value is just the scheme, host, and port of the requesting page — no path, no query. The server compares it against its allowlist and echoes an allowed value back in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. Page JavaScript cannot set or forge `Origin`; it is a forbidden header name, which is what makes it trustworthy to the server.
query.title: The Origin request header

questions.prompt: Which X-Frame-Options value blocks framing by every origin, including the page's own?

choices.rationale: SAMEORIGIN still lets a page on the same origin embed the document in a frame.
This is not a standard value; browsers that treat it as anything allow framing rather than block it.
This grants framing to the named origin instead of blocking everyone.

query.explanation: DENY refuses framing by any page at all. SAMEORIGIN still permits same-origin framing, and values like ALLOWALL simply are not valid defenses.
query.title: X-Frame-Options values

questions.prompt: Can a page sent with the policy below be framed by another page on its own origin?

query.explanation: 'none' matches no source at all, so no document may embed the page — not even one from the identical origin. 'self' is the value that permits same-origin framing.
query.title: frame-ancestors 'none'

questions.rationale: 'none' matches no origin whatsoever, so same-origin framing is refused too; only 'self' would allow it.

questions.prompt: Which CSP directive states which origins may embed this page in a frame?

choices.rationale: frame-src restricts the URLs this page may load inside its own frames, not who may frame it.
child-src is the older fallback for frames and workers this page creates, not for its embedders.
sandbox applies sandbox restrictions to the page itself; it does not list permitted embedders.

query.explanation: frame-ancestors controls who may embed this document. frame-src and child-src control the opposite direction: what this page may load into its own frames.
query.title: Framing directives in CSP

questions.prompt: Does the sandbox attribute on the iframe below list allow-same-origin?

query.explanation: The sandbox attribute is an allowlist of tokens. Only the tokens actually written are granted, so allow-same-origin is absent and the frame keeps an opaque origin.
query.title: Reading sandbox tokens

questions.rationale: Only allow-scripts and allow-forms are present; sandbox grants nothing beyond the tokens written in the attribute.

questions.prompt: What does this code log in a top-level page?

choices.rationale: false would mean the document sits inside a frame, where top refers to a different window.
A strict comparison always evaluates to a boolean, never undefined.
Both window.top and window.self exist on every window, so no error is thrown.

query.explanation: In a document that is not framed, window.top and window.self are the same window object, so the comparison is true. Inside a frame they differ.
query.title: Detecting framing

questions.prompt: Which directive lets only https://app.example.com frame a page from https://example.com?

choices.rationale: 'self' matches https://example.com, the page's own origin, and not the app subdomain.
'none' blocks every embedder, including the intended one.
The wildcard allows any site to frame the page, not just one origin.

query.explanation: Listing the exact origin permits just that embedder. 'self' permits the page's own origin, 'none' permits nobody, and * permits every site.
query.title: Choosing a frame-ancestors source

questions.prompt: Which X-Frame-Options value do modern browsers ignore entirely?

choices.rationale: DENY is the standard value and is honoured by every modern browser.
SAMEORIGIN is still supported and restricts framing to the page's own origin.
The value is case-insensitive, so lowercase deny behaves just like DENY.

query.explanation: ALLOW-FROM was never widely implemented and is dropped by current browsers; use CSP frame-ancestors instead. The token itself is case-insensitive, so lowercase deny still works.
query.title: Obsolete X-Frame-Options syntax

questions.prompt: Do browsers honour X-Frame-Options when it is delivered in the tag below?

query.explanation: X-Frame-Options is only effective as an HTTP response header. A meta http-equiv copy is ignored, unlike Content-Security-Policy, which browsers do accept in meta.
query.title: X-Frame-Options must be a real header

questions.rationale: Only a few http-equiv values such as content-security-policy are honoured; X-Frame-Options must arrive as a real response header.

questions.prompt: Which capability stays blocked inside the iframe below?

choices.rationale: allow-scripts is listed, so script execution is restored inside the frame.
allow-forms is listed, so the frame may submit forms.
Sandbox grants only the tokens present, and allow-popups is not among them.

query.explanation: A sandbox attribute removes all privileges and restores only the listed ones. Scripts and form submission are re-enabled; popups remain blocked because allow-popups is missing.
query.title: Sandbox is an allowlist

choices.rationale: No img element is created, because textContent inserts the string as text rather than parsing it as markup.
Nothing is parsed at all, so there are no child elements, let alone two.
children is always a live HTMLCollection on an element, so length is a number here, not undefined.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

query.explanation: Assigning to textContent stores the string as literal text: the HTML parser is never invoked, so no element nodes are created and div.children stays empty (length 0). The markup is visible to the user as the characters '' rather than being parsed into an img element, so the onerror handler never exists and cannot fire. This is why textContent (or createTextNode) is the safe sink for untrusted strings, while innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML and document.write parse their input as markup and can introduce DOM XSS.
query.title: textContent is not an HTML sink

choices.rationale: The loop returns on the first exact name match, so the later duplicate "theme=blue" is never reached.
"light" belongs to the cookie named themeMode, and the key comparison uses === so themeMode never matches "theme".
null is only returned when no pair's key equals the name, but "theme=dark" matches on the first iteration.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

query.explanation: document.cookie is a single string of name=value pairs joined by "; ". The helper splits on "; ", then splits each pair on "=" and compares the name with ===, so "themeMode" is not treated as a match for "theme". Because it returns on the first exact name match, the first "theme" pair wins and the duplicate "theme=blue" later in the string is never reached. Duplicate cookie names are legal (they can come from different Domain or Path scopes), and the cookie string carries no scope information, so a parser like this silently picks one value. That ambiguity is why security-relevant cookies should be scoped carefully and, where possible, kept out of JavaScript entirely with HttpOnly.
query.title: Reading a value out of a cookie string

choices.rationale: This keeps the frame in its own origin instead of a unique opaque one; it does not re-enable form submission.
Correct: form submission is blocked by sandbox unless allow-forms is listed.
Already present in the attribute, and it only re-enables JavaScript execution, not form submission.
This only lets the frame navigate the top-level browsing context; forms stay blocked.

questions.prompt: Which sandbox token must be added so forms in the iframe below can submit?

query.explanation: A sandbox attribute starts by blocking almost everything: scripts, forms, popups, top navigation, plugins, and same-origin identity. Each listed token adds one capability back. The frame here lists allow-scripts and allow-popups, so scripts run and popups open, but any <form> submission is still blocked until allow-forms is added.
query.title: iframe sandbox re-enables features one token at a time
